pages.x: Krakatoa was a green volcanic island in the Sunda Strait, between Java and Sumatra in the Dutch East Indies. In May 1883 it began to rumble and throw out ash. Passing ships and people on the coasts watched it all summer, more curious than afraid; one steamer even took sightseers out to look.

On the morning of 27 August four huge explosions tore the island apart, and two thirds of it vanished. The last was heard nearly 5,000 kilometres away, on the island of Rodrigues near Mauritius, like the roar of distant guns. It was probably the loudest sound in recorded history.

The explosions and the collapse of the island raised waves up to 30 metres high that smashed into the coasts of Java and Sumatra and swept away 165 towns and villages. A Dutch gunboat was carried far inland and left in the forest.
pages.of: people died, most of them drowned

pages.x: An undersea telegraph cable linked Java to the world, and the news reached newspapers in Europe and America within hours.
pages.fx: It was one of the first disasters the whole world followed almost as it happened, and reports sent in from everywhere gave scientists their first picture of how one volcano can touch the whole planet.

pages.x: Ash and gas thrown high into the sky circled the globe. For months sunsets glowed blood red as far away as Europe and America; near New York fire engines were called out to what looked like a great fire on the horizon. The world was a little cooler for several years.

Some scientists think the blood-red sky in Edvard Munch's painting The Scream, of 1893, remembers the Krakatoa sunsets he saw in Norway as a young man. Munch wrote of a walk at sunset when the sky suddenly turned red as blood. Others say the colours came from his mind, not the sky.

In 1927 a new volcano rose out of the sea where Krakatoa had stood. Named Anak Krakatau, the child of Krakatoa, it has kept growing and erupting, and in 2018 part of it slid into the sea and raised a tsunami that killed more than 400 people.

Krakatoa was not the biggest eruption of its century, Tambora in 1815 was bigger, but it was the first to be studied around the world, and it showed how a single volcano could darken skies and cool the planet. It is still the name people think of for a volcano that explodes.
pts: Its waves killed more than 36,000 people
